title: How Much Can Language Models Gainfrom Test-Time Computation?

paper.title: How Much Can Language Models Gain from Test-Time Computation?
paper.abstract:
Abstract How much can test-time computation improve a language model, and at what cost?
Test-time scaling is widely proposed as a substitute for larger models, but existing comparisons mostly evaluate one domain at a time and rarely charge selection to the budget.
We introduce SELF-POT , a benchmark and evaluation framework that measures the test-time potential of a model across competition mathematics, competitive programming, and agentic workflows. SELF-POT separates candidate coverage from final accuracy on static tasks, tracks correctness transitions under revision, and measures protocol completion alongside task success in agentic environments.
Under a unified budget rule, it compares Direct inference with parallel sampling and self-revision under fixed multiples of the Direct budget, and charges every model call, including selection and critique, in dollars.
This design supports two kinds of comparison: the gain a model obtains from additional inference, and a lower-cost model with additional inference against a stronger model.
Across five low-cost reasoning models on 350 sealed tasks, with Claude Opus 5.5 Direct as the reference, the returns depend on the domain, the selection rule, and failure handling.
When we replay the retained programming candidate pools, public-example selection raises correct submissions from 376 to 453 of 500 scheduled cells while saving 12–49% of logical API cost across models, and simply retaining an available candidate when judging fails recovers 61 submissions at unchanged cost.
On identical mathematics pools, judging with fallback yields 186 correct submissions versus 182 for voting, while voting saves 12–21% of logical API cost.
These controlled replays show how selection and failure handling change the gains realized from the same generated candidates, and they quantify the marginal value of a model judge.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves a fixed language model by spending more computation at inference rather than on training. Parallel methods draw several candidate answers and keep one, chosen by majority vote [ 52 ] , by running candidate programs on tests [ 6 ] , or by a model that judges the candidates [ 12 ] . Sequential methods let the model critique an earlier answer and then revise it [ 36 ] . When the computation is allocated well, a smaller model can match a much larger one on problems it already solves some of the time [ 47 ] , so test-time scaling looks like a way for a low-cost model to replace a stronger and more expensive one. For a fixed model and budget, a practitioner must therefore choose among a single attempt, parallel sampling with selection, and self-revision, and the right choice is unlikely to be the same across tasks. The options differ in what they cost: voting and public-example selection use no additional model tokens, whereas a model judgment can cost as much as another answer. They also differ in what a task permits: in an app workflow, actions can change the environment, so a flawed attempt cannot simply be discarded and drawn again. Figure 1 : SELF-POT : frozen protocol matrix. Each quarter (equal angles) is one domain of the 350-task sealed test set, with its sampling strata in the inner ring. Bars show each low-cost model’s Direct accuracy (%), markers the same model under the TTS protocols, and arcs Claude Opus 5.5 answering once. A marker beyond the end of a bar is a gain, and a marker inside a bar is a loss. Prior comparisons of test-time scaling methods do not tell a practitioner which option to choose in a given task domain. Several studies compare parallel and sequential methods under a matched budget [ 47 , 53 , 51 ] , but they leave three gaps. First, most evaluate a single domain, usually mathematics [ 47 , 21 ] , so a method that helps there may or may not help elsewhere. Second, few charge selection or verification calls to the same budget as generation [ 51 , 46 ] , and most count the budget in FLOPs, samples, or tokens rather than in money. Third, the comparison that motivates test-time scaling, a low-cost model with more computation against a stronger model answering once, has been made only in narrow settings. Snell et al. [47] and Wu et al. [53] compare a smaller and a larger model from the same family (e.g., Llemma-7B and Llemma-34B in the latter) at matched FLOPs and mainly on mathematics. Stroebl et al. [49] compare a weaker and a stronger model on programming tasks. Neither setting measures the comparison in dollars or across domains. We therefore ask three questions: RQ1 Under stated budget allowances, which tested parallel and sequential configurations turn extra computation into accuracy, and in which domains? RQ2 On static tasks, is opportunity lost in generating a correct candidate, selecting it, or preserving it under revision, and do agent protocols complete their intended execution? RQ3 Can a low-cost model with test-time scaling reach the accuracy of a stronger model answering once at no greater cost, and in which cases can it not? Answering these questions places four requirements on an evaluation. It must charge every call, including selection and critique, while keeping the model fixed across roles; it must distinguish the number of candidates, the rule that chooses among them, and the handling of failed stages; its domains must differ in the feedback they provide and in whether actions can be undone; and its test set must be fixed before any test-time call. SELF-POT is built to meet these requirements (Figure 2 ). It gives a frozen model a budget of one, two, or four times a single answer and compares answering once ( Direct ) with two parallel protocols and one sequential protocol, each in the simplest form that a reasoning model can run by itself. Parallel@2 keeps one of two answers by majority vote in mathematics or by the public examples given in a programming task, Parallel@4 lets the same model read three answers and pick one in a selection stage ( joint selection ), and Revise@4 critiques the answer and then revises it. On agent tasks, the parallel protocols compare plans before a single execution ( plan-level parallelism ), and Revise@4 reviews the trajectory every two steps ( periodic self-review ). We evaluate five low-cost reasoning models on 350 tasks in competition mathematics (APEX and Omni-MATH [ 4 , 37 , 20 ] ), AtCoder programming from LiveCodeBench [ 27 ] , AppWorld workflows [ 50 ] , and Terminal-Bench tasks [ 38 ] , fixed and hashed before any evaluation run (a sealed test set), and compare them with Claude Opus 5.5 answering once, the stronger reference model (the anchor ). The five models are DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, GLM-5, GPT-OSS-120B, and MiniMax M2.5. Beyond the protocol comparison, we replay alternative selection and fallback rules on the saved candidate pools, which separates generating a correct candidate from converting it into a correct submission. Figure 1 summarizes the frozen protocol matrix, and our main findings are: • Failure handling can reverse the measured gain. Programming joint selection loses 8.6 percentage points (pp) against Direct under the frozen submission rule; retaining the first available candidate when no nonempty choice is returned turns this into a 3.6 pp gain at unchanged cost (§ 3.3 ). • Public evidence can convert more of the same candidates. On programming, public-example selection yields 453 correct submissions versus 376 for judging, at 12–49% lower API cost. On identical mathematics pools, judging with fallback reaches 186/292 versus 182/292 for voting (§ 3.3 ). • Agent gains require completed protocols. Workflow stage failures reach 117/160 for GPT-OSS and 159/160 for MiniMax, so these configurations primarily measure interface reliability; they do not establish the value of completed plan comparison (§ 3.3 ). • Deployment value differs from within-model gain. Flash Direct remains the coding frontier after the replays are added, and discounted mathematics vote@3 adds a cheaper operating point than judging. Outside programming, Opus remains the most accurate of the tested configurations (§ 3.4 ). Our contributions are: (1) a measurement protocol that holds the model, information, and grading fixed, caps total output at stated multiples of one attempt, and charges every call (§ 2 ); (2) a sealed four-domain test set whose tasks pass a model-independent eligibility check (§ 2.4 ); (3) an evaluation of five low-cost models and a stronger anchor, per model and pooled, with the cost of every configuration (§ 3 ); and (4) controlled candidate-pool replays that separate selection quality, submission failures, and the cost of deployable alternatives (§ 3.3 ). We do not propose a new test-time scaling method. The protocols share one accounting rule, although the feedback available to them and their realized costs differ across domains, and the same-pool replays isolate selection and failure handling on static tasks.

sections.heading: 2 Methodology
sections.text: SELF-POT measures how much additional inference a model turns into final task success, and whether the resulting accuracy justifies its measured API cost. The same frozen model supplies every role within a configuration—solver, selector, critic, and agent—and every call it makes is charged. Figure 2 : SELF-POT protocols. One frozen low-cost model answers the same task under four protocols whose total output is capped at a multiple of the budget B B of one answer, and every call is charged. On agent tasks, the parallel protocols compare plans that are executed once, and Revise@4 reviews the trajectory every two steps (§ 2.2 ). The mathematics problem is illustrative.

sections.heading: 2.1 Measured quantity and budget
sections.text: We measure A ⁡ ( ℳ , π , D , I , E , H , B ) A(\mathcal{M},\pi;\,D,I,E,H,B) , the expected final success rate of model ℳ \mathcal{M} under protocol π \pi , given the task distribution D D , the information I I visible to the solver, the environment E E , the harness H H , and the budget B B . We call the gains attainable under these stated conditions the model’s test-time potential . The measured rate estimates A A for the stated configuration, rather than an intrinsic property of the model. One execution of a protocol on a task by a model is a cell . For domain d d , let B d B_{d} be the Direct output-token allowance and m π m_{\pi} the protocol multiplier. All model calls c 1 , … , c T c_{1},\ldots,c_{T} in a cell obey ∑ t = 1 T τ ⁡ ( c t ) ≤ m π ​ B d , \sum_{t=1}^{T}\tau(c_{t})\leq m_{\pi}B_{d}, (1) where τ \tau counts reasoning and answer tokens. B d B_{d} is 131,072 tokens for mathematics and programming and 393,216 for an agent episode, and the caps on model calls, tool calls, and wall-clock time scale with m π m_{\pi} in the same way (Appendix A ). These are maximum allowances, not matched realized costs: a protocol may stop early, and provider limits can impose tighter stage caps. We therefore report accuracy together with realized token use and dollar cost; the configurations do not constitute a full accuracy–budget response curve.

sections.heading: 2.2 Protocols
sections.text: Direct answers once with the allowance B d B_{d} . On programming, a Direct attempt may run its program on the public examples before submitting it, and on agent tasks it is a complete multi-call episode, so Direct is neither a short answer nor a single request. We do not shorten Direct to create headroom for another method.

sections.heading: Static tasks.
sections.text: Parallel@2 generates two candidates and keeps one by a rule that uses no model tokens: the majority final answer in mathematics and the most public examples passed in programming. Ties go to the earlier candidate, so with two parsed answers voting cannot improve on the first; we therefore also compare three-way voting with judging on identical pools (§ 2.3 ). Parallel@4 generates three candidates and allocates another B B to a joint-selection stage: the same model reads all three and names one, with public-tool calls available on code. Revise@4 runs one Self-Refine iteration [ 36 ] . The model first critiques its answer without writing a new one, a PASS verdict returns the initial answer, and otherwise the model revises it with up to 2 ​ B 2B tokens. The suffix denotes a budget cap, not a sample count, so Parallel@4 and Revise@4 share the cap but not their realized cost. We omit revision at 2 ​ B 2B because our allocation gives each of its three stages a full allowance (Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Agent tasks.
sections.text: Actions change the environment, so no agent protocol resets an episode or chooses among executed worlds. Parallel@ k k with k ∈ { 2 , 4 } k\in\{2,4\} drafts k k plans from the initial observation, selects one with a same-model call, and executes only that plan in a single episode. Revise@4 inserts a same-model review after every two executor turns, appends its advice to the history, and continues from the current state. Planning and plan selection run at low reasoning effort and execution and review at high effort, with all stages sharing the cell’s allowance (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 2.3 From candidate coverage to final accuracy
sections.text: For a protocol that selects from a recorded pool of candidates, let O O indicate that at least one candidate passes the hidden grader and S S that the final submission is correct. Since the submission must be one of the candidates, 𝔼 ⁡ [ S ] = P ⁡ ( O ) ​ P ​ ( S ∣ O ) , \mathbb{E}[S]=P(O)\,P(S\mid O), (2) the product of candidate coverage and conversion . We partition covered failures into two kinds: the selection returns no valid index ( no choice ), or it indexes a candidate that grades incorrect, including an empty candidate ( wrong choice ). Coverage uses hidden grades, so it is an offline ceiling for the recorded candidates rather than a deployable oracle. To isolate conversion, we replay task-appropriate choice rules on the saved Parallel@4 pools: majority voting over three mathematics answers and public-example selection over three programs, each with an earliest-candidate tie rule. We also assess a deterministic fallback that retains the first nonempty candidate when judging yields no usable answer. These post-hoc analyses hold generation fixed and are not new equal-cost trials. Public examples were available to the model judge as well, and hidden grades are used only to score the resulting choices. Fallback retains the already-incurred judge cost, whereas a rule that omits judging excludes that stage’s cost (Appendix J.2 ). For revision, let p p be the accuracy of the protocol’s own initial answers, r r the fraction of initially incorrect submissions that become correct, and d d the fraction of correct answers lost in the final submission. Then Δ = ( 1 − p ) ​ r − p ​ d , \Delta=(1-p)\,r-p\,d, (3) so for r + d > 0 r+d>0 revision gains exactly when p < r / ( r + d ) p<r/(r+d) . These transitions include empty submissions, and we distinguish output failures from changes to completed answers. Unchosen agent plans are never executed, so coverage is undefined for agent protocols, which we compare on the same task across separate episodes rather than through repairs within one trajectory. Both identities are elementary accounting; their value lies in locating where an opportunity is lost.

sections.heading: 2.4 Test set
sections.text: The mathematics problems come from APEX [ 4 , 37 ] and Omni-MATH [ 20 ] , the programming problems from AtCoder through LiveCodeBench v6 [ 27 ] , and the agent tasks from AppWorld [ 50 ] and Terminal-Bench [ 38 ] (Table 1 ). The domains differ in the feedback available while solving and in whether actions can be undone. Mathematics gives no feedback, programming gives execution on the public examples, and the two agent domains return API responses or shell output from an environment whose changes persist. Table 1: The four domains of the sealed test set. Hidden answers, tests, and goal checks are used only for grading; Appendix B gives the sampling strata. Domain Source Tasks Feedback while solving Actions reversible Math APEX [ 4 , 37 ] , Omni-MATH [ 20 ] 60 none yes Code LiveCodeBench v6 [ 27 ] (AtCoder) 100 public examples and execution yes Workflow AppWorld [ 50 ] 160 app API responses no Terminal Terminal-Bench 4.0 [ 38 ] 30 shell output no Tasks pass a model-independent eligibility check: where a reference solution exists, it must pass and a blank or no-op submission must fail under the pinned runtime. Every task seen by a model during development was excluded, and the held-out tasks were drawn within difficulty strata with a fixed seed and at most one task per leakage group, then sealed before any test-time call (Appendix B ). No test item was chosen for an observed test-time gain. Task type, difficulty, feedback, and protocol instantiation change together across domains, so a contrast between domains does not isolate any one of these factors.

sections.heading: 2.5 Grading and cost accounting
sections.text: Mathematics uses a rule-based expression grader, programming runs hidden tests, and workflow and terminal cells use their benchmarks’ native final-state evaluators (Appendix E ). An absent or ungradable submission counts as incorrect, including the 15 scheduled cells that have no final record. For agents, the native grade of the final state is authoritative even when an episode stops at a resource limit, and we report termination status separately. Selection, critique, planning, review, and execution calls all count toward the cell’s allowance and cost. Identical requests may reuse stored responses across static protocols, but every configuration is charged the logical cost of its own calls. Reported costs are mean logical API costs over retained cells at the configured rates, not invoices: DeepSeek is charged at its peak rate, with a half-price scenario where it matters, and Bedrock models at list rates (Bedrock prompt-cache discounts apply only to Opus agent requests). Model outcomes are never retried; bounded infrastructure retries and interface amendments made after sealing are documented in Appendix H .

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: Five lower-priced reasoning models—DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, GLM-5, GPT-OSS-120B, and MiniMax M2.5—are compared with Claude Opus 5.5 Direct as the stronger anchor (Table 2 ; Appendix I ). “Lower-priced” refers to token rates, not to cost per solved task. Only Flash and Qwen3-Next run revision, because the other models’ context windows cannot hold a full-budget critique on top of an answer. GPT-OSS and MiniMax run only Direct on terminal tasks, an adaptive omission after their zero Direct scores; these unrun cells are not counted as failures. sections.heading: Statistics.
sections.text: Each cell is sampled once. Within a model and domain, we count paired wins (protocol correct, Direct incorrect) and losses and apply an exact two-sided sign test, Holm-corrected across all 44 protocol-versus-Direct comparisons. For a pooled domain estimate, we average the paired change over the fixed panel of evaluated models and resample tasks within the frozen strata, keeping all models’ outcomes on a task together (20,000 replicates, pointwise 95% intervals; Appendix J ).

sections.heading: 3.3 RQ2: Converting candidate coverage into task success
sections.text: Figure 4 : Candidate coverage and conversion under frozen Parallel@4. Each bar partitions scheduled tasks. White numbers count correct submissions, labels above bars count covered tasks, and black ticks mark Direct accuracy. “No choice” denotes no valid index; “wrong choice” includes selecting an empty candidate. Same-pool alternatives are compared in Figure 5 and Appendix J.2 . Figure 5 : Same-pool choices and logical API cost. sections.heading: Coverage does not guarantee a correct submission.
sections.text: Figure 4 separates generation from conversion in Parallel@4. In mathematics, Qwen3-Next generates a correct candidate for 38 tasks but submits only 30 correctly, and each lost opportunity is a wrong choice. In programming, GLM-5 covers 88 tasks but submits 55 correctly; missing choices account for most of the gap (27 of the 33 lost pools). In these cases the additional computation has already produced useful answers, and the remaining question is how to deliver them.

sections.heading: Selection and fallback recover much of this potential.
sections.text: On the same programming pools, retaining the first nonempty candidate when judging yields no answer raises correct submissions from 376 to 437 of 500 scheduled cells (Figure 5 ). This alone reverses the mean change against Direct from − 8.6 -8.6 to + 3.6 +3.6 pp, with the judge’s cost still charged. Public-example selection yields 453/500 ( + 6.8 +6.8 pp against Direct), converting 453 of 457 covered pools while saving 12–49% of logical API cost across models. Selection also adds value beyond preserving an output: among the 98 pools with both correct and incorrect candidates, it solves 94 versus 78 for fallback (16 paired wins, no losses). In mathematics, judging with the same fallback yields 186 correct submissions on 292 retained pools, compared with 182 for vote@3. This smaller observed difference has a paired interval spanning zero, while voting saves 12–21% of API cost. Grading sensitivity, per-model counts, uncertainty, and accounting details appear in Appendix J.2 . Finding 2. Candidate coverage becomes useful performance through task-appropriate selection and reliable submission. Programming’s apparent TTS loss reverses with answer-preserving fallback, and public examples recover nearly all recorded coverage. The smaller mathematics difference shows why a judge’s marginal value must be measured against a cheaper choice rule.

sections.heading: Revision and protocol execution.
sections.text: Revision likewise requires separating content changes from lost submissions. Flash’s two mathematics recoveries comprise one repaired answer and one recovered empty output, and Qwen3-Next changes one correct answer to a wrong one. Flash’s sole coding loss follows a truncated critique and an empty final submission; retaining its completed initial program restores the score at unchanged cost. Lower revision accuracy alone therefore does not establish that a correct answer was rewritten incorrectly (Appendix J ). For agents, missing plans or malformed choices frequently prevent the GPT-OSS and MiniMax workflow protocols from reaching execution (Appendix J.1 ). These outcomes measure the model–protocol–interface combination and leave the quality of unexecuted plans unresolved. Finding 3. Agent completion and plan quality remain separate questions. Frequent pre-execution failures prevent judging the value of a functioning multi-plan strategy. Static fallback does not transfer to a changed environment, so agent interface validation and repeated episodes remain necessary. Figure 6 : Cost and accuracy of the frozen configurations; rings mark their Pareto frontier. Selector replays are compared separately in Figure 5 . Costs are mean logical API costs per task over retained cells (DeepSeek peak rates; Bedrock list rates, with Bedrock caching only for Opus agent requests). Code uses the official grades (Opus 93%, 99% with numpy ), and very low workflow costs can reflect early protocol failures. The frontiers are point estimates, not certified dominance relations.

sections.heading: Within-model gains and deployment value are different tests.
sections.text: Figure 6 places every frozen configuration by its mean cost and accuracy. Opus 5.5 Direct leads in mathematics (57/60 against Flash’s best 52/60), workflows (148/160 against 82/160), and terminal tasks (13/30 against 3/30). In programming, GPT-OSS Parallel@2 exceeds the anchor’s frozen score (97 against 93) but costs more ($0.052 against $0.028), while Flash Direct scores 99/100 at $0.013. Supplying the anchor’s missing numpy dependency raises it to 99/100 without new inference (Appendix H ), so GPT-OSS’s advantage is runtime-dependent. Flash Direct still dominates the tested coding replays in API cost and observed accuracy.

sections.heading: The mathematics trade-off changes with the price paid.
sections.text: At peak rates, Flash judging (52/60, $0.176/task) and vote@3 (50/60, $0.144) are both dominated by Opus Direct (57/60, $0.103). At half price, they cost $0.088 and $0.072 and both lie on the expanded frontier. The replay thus adds a cheaper operating point, and judging buys two further correct answers (Appendix J.2 ). Finding 4. Whether test-time scaling pays off depends on the alternatives and on the price basis. Coding replays substantially improve several models without displacing Flash Direct. Discounted mathematics inference adds accuracy–cost trade-offs while remaining below the stronger reference. The choice depends on the model, selector, runtime, and price.

sections.heading: Test-time potential is a conversion profile.
sections.text: The most informative distinction in our measurements is between producing a correct candidate and successfully submitting it. Qwen3-Next’s mathematics coverage exceeds its Direct accuracy while judging does not. GLM-5’s 88 covered programming pools produce 55 correct submissions under the original judge, 78 with nonempty fallback, and 87 with public-example selection. An aggregate gain alone would hide these opportunities, and an aggregate loss alone would conflate wrong decisions with stages that return no decision. Separating coverage, conversion, and revision transitions by output availability makes these cases distinguishable without proposing a new composite score. The contribution is therefore a concrete measurement framework and its cross-domain evidence, rather than a claim that one protocol realizes all of a model’s potential.

sections.heading: Improve the limiting stage before increasing its allowance.
sections.text: The coding results motivate making stage completion an explicit design objective: most losses against Direct occur without a usable final selection. Returning a completed candidate when judging fails recovers 61 coding submissions without new inference, which exposes an avoidable failure-handling loss rather than a limit of candidate generation. For models such as Qwen3-Next in mathematics, however, the selection stage completes and still discards correct candidates, so the relevant target is decision quality. This distinction sharpens the connection to work separating sampling from selection [ 5 ] and examining feedback in self-correction [ 26 , 28 ] .

sections.heading: Measure a judge against a cheaper choice rule.
sections.text: On programming, public-example selection converts 453 of the 457 covered pools, improving on the frozen judge while avoiding its API cost, and it chooses better within pools of mixed correctness rather than merely retaining an answer (Appendix J.2 ). A public-first gate that consults the judge only on public-score ties still calls it on 465 of 498 retained pools, because scores often tie, and yields 452 correct submissions. Public evidence is thus useful even when incomplete, and in these pools the extra judge does not improve on the earliest-best tie rule; this is evidence about the tested selector, not about all possible judges or learned verifiers. On mathematics, judging yields three more correct submissions than voting on identical pools, or four with nonempty fallback, and both paired intervals cross zero, while removing the judge saves 12–21% of the judge-based configuration’s logical API cost. The saved Compass judgments preserve the direction of the difference, with 194 correct submissions for judging with fallback versus 189 for voting (Appendix J.2 ), but neither grader establishes equivalence between the selectors.

sections.heading: Choosing a method is also choosing a model and a runtime.
sections.text: A deployment decision should compare an entire configuration—model, protocol, harness, and price—against the available alternatives. GLM-5’s sizeable coding gain is valuable evidence about its response to inference, yet a cheaper Flash Direct configuration solves more tasks. After incorporating the replays, Flash Direct remains the coding frontier. In mathematics, the discounted replays add operating points: at half price, Flash vote@3 reaches 50/60 at $0.072/task and judging 52/60 at $0.088, whereas at peak rates both are dominated by Opus Direct. The anchor’s coding sensitivity to one missing library further shows why a performance difference should not automatically be interpreted as a capability difference. These observations connect the scientific question of attainable gains to a practical decision: whether to spend the next unit of budget on another candidate, a more reliable selection mechanism, or a different base model.

sections.heading: What should be reported in a TTS evaluation.
sections.text: Our results motivate reporting the Direct operating point and actual resource use, candidate coverage and availability where observable, the outcome of each selection stage, revision transitions, and final native grades alongside termination status. The budget cap and the measured cost answer different questions, and both should be visible. A stronger Direct reference makes deployment claims assessable, while explicit runtime and price sensitivity analyses prevent an incidental environment or tariff from becoming a general conclusion. For agent protocols, unexecuted plans do not provide an oracle coverage estimate; additional controlled executions would be required to separate plan quality from execution reliability.

sections.heading: Test-time scaling.
sections.text: Parallel methods generate several candidates and select one, with a trained verifier that scores answers or reasoning steps [ 13 , 34 , 57 , 42 ] or without one, by majority vote [ 52 , 10 ] , by executing programs on tests that the model writes [ 6 ] , or by letting the model judge the candidates [ 12 , 58 ] . Selection often limits the gains: coverage keeps rising with more samples while voting and reward-model selection level off [ 5 ] , an imperfect verifier caps the accuracy that resampling can reach [ 49 ] , and verification draws on the generation budget [ 46 ] . Sequential methods revise an earlier attempt [ 36 ] . Without external feedback, self-correction rarely improves reasoning and can turn correct answers into wrong ones [ 26 , 48 , 28 ] , whereas feedback from tools, execution, or the environment [ 22 , 11 , 45 ] and a model trained to revise [ 47 ] help more, at a cost that can offset the gain [ 40 ] . Reasoning models also check their work inside one long chain of thought [ 39 ] , which beyond a point does worse than parallel sampling at the same budget [ 21 , 56 ] , and tree search [ 54 ] and debate [ 18 ] combine the two families. SELF-POT runs the simplest verifier-free form of each family that a reasoning model can execute by itself.

sections.heading: Controlled comparisons.
sections.text: Several studies compare test-time scaling methods under a matched budget (Table 5 ). In mathematics, a smaller model given more inference compute can match or surpass a larger one on questions it already solves at a non-trivial rate, and voting saturates as samples grow [ 47 , 53 ] . Across single-turn reasoning tasks, self-consistency frequently outperforms more elaborate strategies at equal budget [ 51 ] , and accuracy can first rise and then fall as the number of calls grows [ 7 ] . For agents, higher reasoning effort gives equal or lower accuracy in 21 of 36 model–agent–benchmark combinations [ 29 ] , and neither sequential nor parallel scaling helps general agents much [ 31 ] . A concurrent report covers mathematics, science questions, and planning across nine models [ 3 ] . None of these studies combines mathematics, programming, and agent tasks with charged selection calls and a comparison against a stronger model, which is the combination SELF-POT provides.

sections.heading: Cost-aware evaluation.
sections.text: Holistic evaluation suites report efficiency in runtime and hardware units [ 33 ] , agent evaluations argue for and adopt joint reporting of dollar cost and accuracy [ 30 , 29 ] , and cost-of-pass measures the expected dollar cost of one correct answer [ 19 ] . Test-time scaling studies mostly count FLOPs [ 47 , 53 ] , yet the unit of cost matters: inference demand changes the compute-optimal model size [ 44 ] , memory-access cost removes much of the apparent advantage of small models under best-of- N N sampling and long reasoning [ 43 ] , and models often reason far longer than a problem requires [ 9 , 24 ] . Cascades and routers instead choose a model for each query [ 8 , 55 , 23 , 1 , 16 , 41 , 15 ] , sometimes together with the number of samples [ 17 ] , and adaptive stopping rules reduce the samples a single model needs [ 2 , 32 , 14 ] . These approaches compare models at their native settings or assume that sampling a cheaper model is the more economical path, an assumption that SELF-POT tests directly.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced SELF-POT , a benchmark and evaluation framework that measures how additional inference becomes task success, and at what cost, across 350 sealed tasks in mathematics, programming, and agentic environments. A recurring lesson is that the most informative distinction lies between producing a correct candidate and successfully submitting it. On fixed programming pools, public-example selection raises correct submissions from 376 to 453, and output-preserving fallback alone recovers 61, so selection and failure handling can reverse an observed TTS loss. In mathematics, judging with fallback adds four correct submissions over cheaper voting, and discounted vote@3 adds a deployment trade-off, while Flash Direct retains the coding frontier. For agents, interfaces require validation before their outcomes can be attributed to planning. Together, these measurements connect candidate coverage, executable selection rules, and cost to the practical question of inference allocation: whether the next unit of budget is better spent on another candidate, a more reliable selection mechanism, or a different base model.

sections.heading: Appendix B Test set construction
sections.text: Tasks were admitted by a model-independent eligibility check, drawn by stratum with a fixed seed, and sealed before any test-time call.

sections.heading: Eligibility.
sections.text: Where an executable reference is distributed, eligibility requires that it succeeds and a blank or no-op submission fails under the pinned runtime. AppWorld uses the separate contract below because its test references are unavailable. For code, an official editorial program must pass every hidden test in our container; duplicate references are removed by code hash. AppWorld’s test split ships no reference solutions, so eligibility there requires the official development examples to pass, the native evaluator chain to be fixed, and a blank state to fail; all 585 test tasks met this contract. For Terminal-Bench, the Harbor oracle agent must obtain reward 1 and the nop agent reward 0; 62 of 66 tasks qualified, three were excluded for requiring GPUs, and one because its reference could not run in the shipped image.

Every task seen by any model during development (math 52, code 25, workflow 15, terminal 1) was excluded, together with three AtCoder contests held out as a whole (abc391, abc398, arc191). The set was sealed on 2026-09-21; the seal records hashes of the specification and of the public and private task files, and the tasks did not change afterwards. sections.heading: Appendix D Protocol details
sections.text: The original protocols require a formatted choice and use no fallback after an unparseable selection. Appendix J.2 evaluates output-preserving alternatives on the same candidates.

sections.heading: Joint selection (Parallel@4, static tasks).
sections.text: The model receives the problem and the three candidates, labelled A to C, and is told to verify each candidate’s decisive steps rather than compare their popularity. It must end with SELECTED: <letter> . If that line is missing but the last boxed expression is a single candidate letter, the choice is accepted and the parse route is recorded, so the strict score remains recomputable; any other reply is a format failure.

sections.heading: Self-Refine (Revise@4, static tasks).
sections.text: The critique prompt forbids a replacement solution and a final answer, asks the model to quote each faulty step and state what should change, and requires VERDICT: PASS or VERDICT: REVISE . A PASS returns the initial solution without a revision call; an unparseable verdict proceeds to revision. If critique fails to finish or revision yields no completed final answer, the frozen harness returns an empty submission without falling back to the initial answer. Appendix J evaluates this implementation choice offline. Whether the feedback asserts an answer different from the initial one is recorded per cell. Relative to Madaan et al. [36] , we run one feedback–refine iteration and no few-shot demonstrations.

sections.heading: Public-test selection (Parallel@2, code).
sections.text: Each candidate program is compiled and run on the public examples; the one matching the most examples is kept, with ties going to the earlier candidate. Compile failures or empty programs receive a penalty below a runnable program that matches no public examples. Hidden tests are never consulted, and the step consumes no model tokens, although it requires executing the candidates.

sections.heading: Agent protocols.
sections.text: For Parallel@ k k , the model proposes k k plans from the initial observation without calling tools, then replies SELECT: N ; an invalid selection ends the cell as a stage failure. The chosen plan is appended to the context and executed once. For Revise@4, after every second executor turn the model is asked to inspect the goal, the visible state, and recent errors, to choose among continuing, inspecting and repairing, replanning, or stopping, to preserve actions that already succeeded, and not to claim success without checking the observable state. The review text is appended to the context; the program does not parse the chosen option, and the episode ends when the executor issues no further tool call.

sections.heading: Protocols not included.
sections.text: A separately instructed longer-reasoning protocol was not run. Direct already uses high effort and a generous allowance, but this does not establish equivalence to all alternative long-reasoning prompts or provider effort settings. Revise at 2 × 2\times is excluded by our choice to allocate a full solution allowance to each of its three stages; other revision allocations remain possible. Domain-specific methods, such as moderated debate for mathematics or test-driven repair for code, were planned as a separate audit and are not part of the reported results.

sections.heading: Appendix E Grading and runtime
sections.text: Static outputs use the declared answer or execution grader, and agents use native final-state evaluators; hidden answers and tests are used only for offline grading. • Math. A rule-based expression grader checks the final scalar answer. An offline CompassVerifier-3B model [ 35 ] grades the same outputs as a second opinion; the two disagree on 25 of 1,069 scored mathematics cells. • Code. Programs run against all hidden tests in a pinned container (image sha256:4a33fba9… ; CPython 3.11; g++ 12.2 with -std=c++20 ; AtCoder Library). Re-running eligibility for all 282 AtCoder candidates under C++20 in the same image added six tasks and removed none. • Workflow. AppWorld’s native evaluator reports task goal completion, which requires every check to pass; we do not call it the official scenario goal completion. • Terminal. Terminal-Bench’s native verifier, run by Harbor in a separate container, returns a binary reward. Following AppWorld’s usage terms, we report only aggregate results on its test split and do not inspect individual test trajectories.

sections.heading: Appendix F Agent harness
sections.text: Agents act through one uniform tool interface per domain, and the harness enforces limits inside the task environment. Each cell begins from the prescribed initial state, with no memory carried across tasks. Agents can change the environment and may sometimes undo individual actions, but the harness forbids branching into cloned worlds, resetting an episode, or selecting among multiple executed worlds. Terminal tasks run in their native Harbor [ 25 ] containers through a single shell-command tool rather than the tmux interface of the reference Terminus-2 agent, so our scores are not comparable to the public leaderboard. A single command is limited to 1,800 s, the longest native verifier timeout in our terminal set. The limit is enforced inside the container and terminates the whole process group; a stopped command returns exit status 124 to the model, and the tool description states the limit. The AppWorld environment server serves one episode at a time. Half of the 160 workflow runs used four replica servers that match the original in image, read-only data, and resource limits and differ only in port; each run records the server it used.

sections.heading: Appendix G Development evidence behind the design
sections.text: Three design rules—full budgets for judges, a judge at the solver’s effort, and verification instead of voting in Parallel@4—were adopted after development measurements, before the test set was sealed. • Observed judging costs. A critique at low effort used 58,173 output tokens, 58,100 of them reasoning, to emit 255 characters; critiques capped at B / 8 B/8 or B / 16 B/16 stopped mid-reasoning and returned no verdict. Selection calls used 14,637–61,719 output tokens. • A low-effort critique error. On a problem the solver answered correctly in three of three attempts, a low-effort critique asserted a different answer as established. • Development selector comparison. On 16 development problems, Direct scored 0.625, majority voting over three samples 0.562, and at least one of three samples was correct 81% of the time. On the seven contested problems, joint verification recovered four of five that had a correct candidate; voting recovered one. Self-verification accepted a wrong solution in 7 of 15 usable judgments. • Eight-sample pilot. On the hardest seven development problems with eight samples each, voting peaked at four samples while coverage kept rising. These small development observations motivated the original design; they do not establish that judging is preferable on held-out tasks. The same-pool test analysis in Appendix J.2 measures that marginal value explicitly.

sections.heading: Appendix H Accounting, failures, and changes after sealing
sections.text: We distinguish logical method cost from campaign spending, task correctness from termination status, and a fixed task seal from versioned implementation amendments.

sections.heading: Cost ledger.
sections.text: Before each call, the ledger reserves the stage cap at the configured price and settles actual usage afterwards; a failed call keeps its reservation. This is conservative for retained calls, but configuration means are not an upper bound on whole-campaign expense: they average retained final cell records and omit superseded infrastructure attempts and records that never completed. Identical requests reused across protocols are charged logically in every configuration, although they are physically paid for only once. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash uses one fixed peak-rate snapshot for every call: $0.30 per million uncached input tokens, $1.20 per million output tokens, and $0.006 per million cache-read tokens. Token counts and cache hits come from the recorded usage; prices do not depend on the call timestamp. The half-price sensitivity multiplies every DeepSeek configuration cost by 0.5, holding usage fixed. Neither scenario reconstructs the actual invoice, although most calls ran off-peak. Bedrock models are charged at list price; Opus 5.5 agent requests use prompt caching, which changes cost but not model inputs or outputs. The GPT-OSS price on the pricing page is the Sydney region’s, so its ledger errs high. An accounting audit recovered 12 Flash terminal cell records whose parent runs had not written an aggregate evaluation file. Their grades were already retained, but the merger had defaulted their costs to zero. We restore the saved costs ($6.20 in total) and token usage, leaving all outcomes unchanged: Direct, Parallel@2, and Parallel@4 cost $0.307, $0.363, and $0.438 per retained task, respectively. The tables and Figure 6 use these corrected values; analysis/audit_terminal_costs.py records the source hashes and correction. Terminal frontier membership is unchanged. Ledger totals are about $101 for DeepSeek (including screening), $282 for Qwen3-Next and GLM-5, $83 for Opus 5.5, and $82 for GPT-OSS and MiniMax.

sections.heading: Failures.
sections.text: Cells with no usable submission or no final record score zero, and model outcomes are not retried to obtain a better answer. For agents, the native evaluator scores the final world state independently of the termination status. The retained matrix includes six correct resource-limited cells: two Flash workflow Direct cells, one Flash terminal Direct cell, one Flash terminal Parallel@4 cell, and two Opus terminal Direct cells. Reporting every non-completed status as incorrect would therefore misdescribe the primary scores. Only infrastructure failures—dropped connections, provider server errors, permission errors, and task containers that failed to start—were resumed or re-run, at most twice per task. Fifteen cells never finished and are scored as incorrect: two Flash terminal cells that reached their wall-clock limit, ten GLM-5 mathematics cells whose Bedrock requests hung until the client timeout (about 5% of GLM-5 requests hung; every successful call finished within 1,798 s), and three GPT-OSS cells whose identical request hung or returned a server error on every retry. Six terminal Direct cells whose Harbor container failed to start or whose command exceeded the operating system’s argument limit were re-run and now have valid grades; two verifier timeouts count as failures, as Terminal-Bench scores them.

sections.heading: Opus 5.5 on code without numpy.
sections.text: Six of Opus 5.5’s seven code failures import numpy, which the frozen grading image does not contain, so these programs fail at import. The prompt states no library restriction, but it offers a tool that runs code in the same sandbox, and Opus 5.5 submitted these six programs without running them; no other model imported numpy. We therefore keep the official score of 0.930. Regrading the six programs in the same image with numpy 2.4.6 installed and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 set makes all six pass, giving 0.990.

sections.heading: Changes after sealing.
sections.text: Four infrastructure changes were made after sealing, and each affected configuration declares it. (i) Terminal tasks run through a native Harbor bridge, including the per-command limit. (ii) Amazon Bedrock’s Converse API rejected three agent-loop situations as validation errors, ending runs for interface reasons: a tool-less review call over a transcript with tool turns, a call to a tool name the model invented, and tool calls written as plain JSON text. The first two are now rendered as text, and calls to declared tools written as text are recovered and marked (24% of Qwen3-Next’s workflow calls and 11% of its terminal calls). (iii) Prompt caching on Bedrock agent requests. (iv) Output caps of selection stages fitted to the remaining context window for models whose window is smaller than the frozen cap. These changes preserve the sealed tasks and primary graders, but they affect tool-history serialization, executable tool handling, or the effective per-request cap. Nominal cell allowances do not imply identical realized inputs and stage limits across interface versions. The Qwen3-Next runs on the earlier interface are retained as an implementation baseline, not pooled into the final matrix.

sections.heading: Appendix I Models
sections.text: Solver and review stages request high reasoning effort; agent planning and plan selection request low effort. Provider-specific limits and interface settings are part of the reported configuration. Table 2 in Section 3.1 lists access, prices, and context windows. Only Flash and Qwen3-Next meet the context-headroom requirement of our full-solution critique configuration; this exclusion does not imply that shorter or differently structured revision is impossible for the other models. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is accessed through the official API with thinking enabled, reasoning effort high, and top- ​ p = 0.95 \text{top-}p=0.95 ; no temperature or seed is sent. The other models are accessed through Amazon Bedrock (us-east-1; Opus 5.5 through the global endpoint with adaptive thinking at effort high). We accept a single-call output limit only when a generation actually stops at that limit, because provider model cards understated capacity for four of eight candidates during screening. Bedrock caps output per call at 128,000 tokens for Opus 5.5 and GPT-OSS, below the nominal 131,072; affected stages are capped explicitly while total cell allowances remain unchanged. Qwen3-Next’s static revision is capped at 131,072 rather than the nominal 262,144, so its three-stage allocation totals at most 3 ​ B 3B under a 4 ​ B 4B cell allowance. GPT-OSS’s 131,072-token window additionally limits its solution stages to 118,000 tokens, which truncated three mathematics candidates, and its selection stages are fitted to the remaining window. On one terminal task, Bedrock’s content filter stopped two of Opus 5.5’s turns, ending the episode; it counts as a model outcome.

sections.text: The audit in analysis/audit_results.py validates the number of retained records and correct outcomes for all 68 configurations against the frozen result matrix before computing diagnostics. It also checks that each task index agrees with the sealed public manifest. Only retained final runs and declared parts are merged; superseded attempts are excluded. AppWorld records are projected to aggregate status and grade counts without inspecting individual trajectories. The output contains aggregate statistics and source hashes, not task text or model answers.

sections.heading: Content changes and missing submissions.
sections.text: The 320 static revision cells contain 68 final failures: 66 initially incorrect submissions remain incorrect, one correct answer becomes an incorrect answer, and one correct initial program is followed by an empty final submission. The content-level loss is Qwen3-Next mathematics: both its initial and revised answers are nonempty and complete. The submission loss is Flash programming: its critique exhausts its 131,072-token stage allowance before revision begins, and the harness discards the correct initial program. Conversely, Flash’s two mathematics W → \to R transitions include one repair of a nonempty wrong answer and one recovery from an initial generation truncated at 131,072 tokens. Thus the operational W → \to R and R → \to W counts do not alone identify content-level repair or damage.

sections.heading: Post-hoc sensitivity: retaining the initial answer.
sections.text: We replay a deterministic fallback on all 320 static revision records: if the cell ends with a stage failure, truncation, or exhausted budget, has no final submission, and has a nonempty completed initial answer, return that initial answer. The trigger uses only termination status and output availability; existing hidden grades score the returned answer but never determine whether fallback occurs. Exactly one cell qualifies, the Flash programming case above, raising its accuracy from 98/100 to 99/100, equal to Direct. All other static revision scores are unchanged, and all spent tokens and logical API costs remain charged. This analysis uses saved outputs and grades without new inference or grading; the frozen primary scores remain unchanged. It isolates one avoidable loss from the failure-handling rule and does not establish that revision preserves correctness in general. The replay does not apply to agent episodes, where actions may already have changed the environment.

sections.heading: Candidate-pool replay.
sections.text: Every retained mathematics Parallel@4 record contains three graded candidates: 60 pools each for Flash, Qwen3-Next, and MiniMax, 53 for GLM-5, and 59 for GPT-OSS. We apply the original final-answer parser and voting tie rule to these same strings, then look up the selected candidate’s existing grade. The choice rule has no access to correctness labels. This isolates the choice rule on observed pools, while the eight missing records remain failures in the primary 60-task denominators. On programming, 496 records contain all three attempt slots, including empty attempts; two GPT-OSS records are partial and two are missing. Coverage of partial pools is reported only when a correct candidate is observed. No unavailable candidate is imputed correct or incorrect for the conditional conversion calculation.

sections.heading: Agents.
sections.text: On workflows, Flash’s small gains under plan-level parallelism (78/160 to 82/160 and 81/160) coexist with losses for GLM-5, GPT-OSS, and MiniMax and near-floor performance for Qwen3-Next. For workflow Parallel@2 and Parallel@4, GPT-OSS records 117/160 and 111/160 stage failures, respectively, and MiniMax records 159/160 under either protocol. The recorded aggregate diagnostics associate these failures with absent final planning messages or tool-call markup in stages that require a plan or a selection. These rows measure end-to-end performance of the model–protocol–interface combination, not the quality of a successfully executed multi-plan strategy. Flash’s workflow review lowers accuracy from 78/160 to 55/160 with 11 paired wins and 34 losses (Holm-adjusted p = 0.033 p=0.033 ); because these are separate episodes, the 34 losses are not observations of an individual trajectory being repaired into failure. On terminal tasks, Flash remains at 3/30 under either Parallel protocol, while Qwen3-Next and GLM-5 remain at zero; Flash nevertheless exchanges solved tasks with Direct, so unchanged accuracy does not mean that the protocols solve identical instances. Thirteen recorded Flash terminal Direct cells and eight Opus terminal Direct cells terminate at a token or call limit, including cases whose final state is nevertheless correct. Across the entire matrix, six resource-limited agent cells pass the native evaluator (Appendix H ); retaining these grades distinguishes task completion from the harness’s stopping condition.

sections.heading: J.2 Same-pool selection and failure-handling replay
sections.text: We compare choice rules on stored candidate strings, using hidden grades only after selection. This post-hoc analysis preserves the frozen primary matrix; it does not add generation samples, replace missing records, or estimate repeated-generation variability. We retain per-pool choices, public execution evidence, stage costs, and input hashes in the replay records; analysis/run_selector_replay.py and analysis/summarize_selector_replay.py reproduce execution and aggregation. Figure 5 in Section 3.3 plots the resulting accuracy against logical API cost.

sections.heading: Programming rules and execution.
sections.text: We process all 498 retained pools: 496 pools with all three attempt slots recorded and two partial GPT-OSS pools. Two missing GPT-OSS records remain wrong in the denominator of 500 scheduled cells. We compare the frozen judge (J), fallback to the first nonempty candidate when J returns no valid nonempty choice (J+F), public-example fallback under the same condition (J+P), and public-example selection on all three candidates (P3) or only the first two of the same pool (P2). Public selection maximizes examples passed and breaks ties by candidate order; an empty or uncompilable candidate receives a negative score. No hidden grade determines selection or fallback. These pools retain empty or truncated attempts as failures; they do not require three usable programs. As further availability-conditioned checks, the 459 pools with three nonempty answers give 354 correct submissions for J versus 423 for P3. The 419 pools where all three candidates compile give 336 versus 392. These descriptive subsets do not replace the scheduled denominator. Public execution reuses the frozen grading helper and immutable runtime image with network disabled, read-only containers, bounded memory, and the original compilation and execution limits. The replay makes 3,959 public-test executions in 838 seconds with four workers (3,299 summed worker-seconds), with no environment errors. Every candidate recorded as hidden-correct passes its public examples. No hidden tests are re-executed, and no new API request is made. These runtime measurements report the local execution expense separately from API dollars.

sections.text: The original index-only fallback recovers 60 correct submissions (436/500). Inspection revealed one further case in which a valid judge index refers to an empty candidate. The output-aware amendment triggers fallback for this public condition as well, giving J+F 437/500 and J+P 440/500, compared with 439/500 for index-only public fallback. This additional rule was specified after that inspection and is reported as post-hoc. J+F therefore recovers 61 submissions at unchanged logical cost, changing the gain against Direct from − 8.6 -8.6 to + 3.6 +3.6 pp. P3 yields 453/500 ( + 6.8 +6.8 pp against Direct), converts 453 of 457 covered pools, and saves 12–49% of logical API cost across models. Bangji Yang Jingyuan Li Jiajun Fan Yi Evie Zhang Ruihan Guo Hongba Ma Neil He Chumeng Liang Qinglong Zheng Zhanghan Ni Ge Liu Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Email: geliu@illinois.edu October 1, 2026 Abstract How much can test-time computation improve a language model, and at what cost? Test-time scaling is widely proposed as a substitute for larger models, but existing comparisons mostly evaluate one domain at a time and rarely charge selection to the budget. We introduce SELF-POT , a benchmark and evaluation framework that measures the test-time potential of a model across competition mathematics, competitive programming, and agentic workflows. SELF-POT separates candidate coverage from final accuracy on static tasks, tracks correctness transitions under revision, and measures protocol completion alongside task success in agentic environments. Under a unified budget rule, it compares Direct inference with parallel sampling and self-revision under fixed multiples of the Direct budget, and charges every model call, including selection and critique, in dollars. This design supports two kinds of comparison: the gain a model obtains from additional inference, and a lower-cost model with additional inference against a stronger model. Across five low-cost reasoning models on 350 sealed tasks, with Claude Opus 5.5 Direct as the reference, the returns depend on the domain, the selection rule, and failure handling. When we replay the retained programming candidate pools, public-example selection raises correct submissions from 376 to 453 of 500 scheduled cells while saving 12–49% of logical API cost across models, and simply retaining an available candidate when judging fails recovers 61 submissions at unchanged cost. On identical mathematics pools, judging with fallback yields 186 correct submissions versus 182 for voting, while voting saves 12–21% of logical API cost. These controlled replays show how selection and failure handling change the gains realized from the same generated candidates, and they quantify the marginal value of a model judge. 1 Introduction Test-time scaling (TTS) improves a fixed language model by spending more computation at inference rather than on training. Parallel methods draw several candidate answers and keep one, chosen by majority vote [ 52 ] , by running candidate programs on tests [ 6 ] , or by a model that judges the candidates [ 12 ] . Sequential methods let the model critique an earlier answer and then revise it [ 36 ] . When the computation is allocated well, a smaller model can match a much larger one on problems it already solves some of the time [ 47 ] , so test-time scaling looks like a way for a low-cost model to replace a stronger and more expensive one. For a fixed model and budget, a practitioner must therefore choose among a single attempt, parallel sampling with selection, and self-revision, and the right choice is unlikely to be the same across tasks. The options differ in what they cost: voting and public-example selection use no additional model tokens, whereas a model judgment can cost as much as another answer. They also differ in what a task permits: in an app workflow, actions can change the environment, so a flawed attempt cannot simply be discarded and drawn again. Figure 1 : SELF-POT : frozen protocol matrix. Each quarter (equal angles) is one domain of the 350-task sealed test set, with its sampling strata in the inner ring. Bars show each low-cost model’s Direct accuracy (%), markers the same model under the TTS protocols, and arcs Claude Opus 5.5 answering once. A marker beyond the end of a bar is a gain, and a marker inside a bar is a loss. Prior comparisons of test-time scaling methods do not tell a practitioner which option to choose in a given task domain. Several studies compare parallel and sequential methods under a matched budget [ 47 , 53 , 51 ] , but they leave three gaps. First, most evaluate a single domain, usually mathematics [ 47 , 21 ] , so a method that helps there may or may not help elsewhere. Second, few charge selection or verification calls to the same budget as generation [ 51 , 46 ] , and most count the budget in FLOPs, samples, or tokens rather than in money. Third, the comparison that motivates test-time scaling, a low-cost model with more computation against a stronger model answering once, has been made only in narrow settings. Snell et al. [47] and Wu et al. [53] compare a smaller and a larger model from the same family (e.g., Llemma-7B and Llemma-34B in the latter) at matched FLOPs and mainly on mathematics. Stroebl et al. [49] compare a weaker and a stronger model on programming tasks. Neither setting measures the comparison in dollars or across domains. We therefore ask three questions: RQ1 Under stated budget allowances, which tested parallel and sequential configurations turn extra computation into accuracy, and in which domains? RQ2 On static tasks, is opportunity lost in generating a correct candidate, selecting it, or preserving it under revision, and do agent protocols complete their intended execution? RQ3 Can a low-cost model with test-time scaling reach the accuracy of a stronger model answering once at no greater cost, and in which cases can it not? Answering these questions places four requirements on an evaluation. It must charge every call, including selection and critique, while keeping the model fixed across roles; it must distinguish the number of candidates, the rule that chooses among them, and the handling of failed stages; its domains must differ in the feedback they provide and in whether actions can be undone; and its test set must be fixed before any test-time call. SELF-POT is built to meet these requirements (Figure 2 ). It gives a frozen model a budget of one, two, or four times a single answer and compares answering once ( Direct ) with two parallel protocols and one sequential protocol, each in the simplest form that a reasoning model can run by itself. Parallel@2 keeps one of two answers by majority vote in mathematics or by the public examples given in a programming task, Parallel@4 lets the same model read three answers and pick one in a selection stage ( joint selection ), and Revise@4 critiques the answer and then revises it. On agent tasks, the parallel protocols compare plans before a single execution ( plan-level parallelism ), and Revise@4 reviews the trajectory every two steps ( periodic self-review ). We evaluate five low-cost reasoning models on 350 tasks in competition mathematics (APEX and Omni-MATH [ 4 , 37 , 20 ] ), AtCoder programming from LiveCodeBench [ 27 ] , AppWorld workflows [ 50 ] , and Terminal-Bench tasks [ 38 ] , fixed and hashed before any evaluation run (a sealed test set), and compare them with Claude Opus 5.5 answering once, the stronger reference model (the anchor ). The five models are DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, GLM-5, GPT-OSS-120B, and MiniMax M2.5. Beyond the protocol comparison, we replay alternative selection and fallback rules on the saved candidate pools, which separates generating a correct candidate from converting it into a correct submission. Figure 1 summarizes the frozen protocol matrix, and our main findings are: • Failure handling can reverse the measured gain. Programming joint selection loses 8.6 percentage points (pp) against Direct under the frozen submission rule; retaining the first available candidate when no nonempty choice is returned turns this into a 3.6 pp gain at unchanged cost (§ 3.3 ). • Public evidence can convert more of the same candidates. On programming, public-example selection yields 453 correct submissions versus 376 for judging, at 12–49% lower API cost. On identical mathematics pools, judging with fallback reaches 186/292 versus 182/292 for voting (§ 3.3 ). • Agent gains require completed protocols. Workflow stage failures reach 117/160 for GPT-OSS and 159/160 for MiniMax, so these configurations primarily measure interface reliability; they do not establish the value of completed plan comparison (§ 3.3 ). • Deployment value differs from within-model gain. Flash Direct remains the coding frontier after the replays are added, and discounted mathematics vote@3 adds a cheaper operating point than judging. Outside programming, Opus remains the most accurate of the tested configurations (§ 3.4 ). Our contributions are: (1) a measurement protocol that holds the model, information, and grading fixed, caps total output at stated multiples of one attempt, and charges every call (§ 2 ); (2) a sealed four-domain test set whose tasks pass a model-independent eligibility check (§ 2.4 ); (3) an evaluation of five low-cost models and a stronger anchor, per model and pooled, with the cost of every configuration (§ 3 ); and (4) controlled candidate-pool replays that separate selection quality, submission failures, and the cost of deployable alternatives (§ 3.3 ). We do not propose a new test-time scaling method. The most informative distinction in our measurements is between producing a correct candidate and successfully submitting it. Qwen3-Next’s mathematics coverage exceeds its Direct accuracy while judging does not. GLM-5’s 88 covered programming pools produce 55 correct submissions under the original judge, 78 with nonempty fallback, and 87 with public-example selection. An aggregate gain alone would hide these opportunities, and an aggregate loss alone would conflate wrong decisions with stages that return no decision. Separating coverage, conversion, and revision transitions by output availability makes these cases distinguishable without proposing a new composite score. The contribution is therefore a concrete measurement framework and its cross-domain evidence, rather than a claim that one protocol realizes all of a model’s potential. Improve the limiting stage before increasing its allowance. The coding results motivate making stage completion an explicit design objective: most losses against Direct occur without a usable final selection. Returning a completed candidate when judging fails recovers 61 coding submissions without new inference, which exposes an avoidable failure-handling loss rather than a limit of candidate generation. For models such as Qwen3-Next in mathematics, however, the selection stage completes and still discards correct candidates, so the relevant target is decision quality. This distinction sharpens the connection to work separating sampling from selection [ 5 ] and examining feedback in self-correction [ 26 , 28 ] . Measure a judge against a cheaper choice rule. On programming, public-example selection converts 453 of the 457 covered pools, improving on the frozen judge while avoiding its API cost, and it chooses better within pools of mixed correctness rather than merely retaining an answer (Appendix J.2 ). A public-first gate that consults the judge only on public-score ties still calls it on 465 of 498 retained pools, because scores often tie, and yields 452 correct submissions. Public evidence is thus useful even when incomplete, and in these pools the extra judge does not improve on the earliest-best tie rule; this is evidence about the tested selector, not about all possible judges or learned verifiers. On mathematics, judging yields three more correct submissions than voting on identical pools, or four with nonempty fallback, and both paired intervals cross zero, while removing the judge saves 12–21% of the judge-based configuration’s logical API cost. The saved Compass judgments preserve the direction of the difference, with 194 correct submissions for judging with fallback versus 189 for voting (Appendix J.2 ), but neither grader establishes equivalence between the selectors. Choosing a method is also choosing a model and a runtime. A deployment decision should compare an entire configuration—model, protocol, harness, and price—against the available alternatives. GLM-5’s sizeable coding gain is valuable evidence about its response to inference, yet a cheaper Flash Direct configuration solves more tasks. After incorporating the replays, Flash Direct remains the coding frontier. In mathematics, the discounted replays add operating points: at half price, Flash vote@3 reaches 50/60 at $0.072/task and judging 52/60 at $0.088, whereas at peak rates both are dominated by Opus Direct. The anchor’s coding sensitivity to one missing library further shows why a performance difference should not automatically be interpreted as a capability difference. These observations connect the scientific question of attainable gains to a practical decision: whether to spend the next unit of budget on another candidate, a more reliable selection mechanism, or a different base model. What should be reported in a TTS evaluation. Our results motivate reporting the Direct operating point and actual resource use, candidate coverage and availability where observable, the outcome of each selection stage, revision transitions, and final native grades alongside termination status. The budget cap and the measured cost answer different questions, and both should be visible. A stronger Direct reference makes deployment claims assessable, while explicit runtime and price sensitivity analyses prevent an incidental environment or tariff from becoming a general conclusion. Sequential methods revise an earlier attempt [ 36 ] . Without external feedback, self-correction rarely improves reasoning and can turn correct answers into wrong ones [ 26 , 48 , 28 ] , whereas feedback from tools, execution, or the environment [ 22 , 11 , 45 ] and a model trained to revise [ 47 ] help more, at a cost that can offset the gain [ 40 ] . Reasoning models also check their work inside one long chain of thought [ 39 ] , which beyond a point does worse than parallel sampling at the same budget [ 21 , 56 ] , and tree search [ 54 ] and debate [ 18 ] combine the two families. SELF-POT runs the simplest verifier-free form of each family that a reasoning model can execute by itself. Controlled comparisons. Several studies compare test-time scaling methods under a matched budget (Table 5 ). In mathematics, a smaller model given more inference compute can match or surpass a larger one on questions it already solves at a non-trivial rate, and voting saturates as samples grow [ 47 , 53 ] . Across single-turn reasoning tasks, self-consistency frequently outperforms more elaborate strategies at equal budget [ 51 ] , and accuracy can first rise and then fall as the number of calls grows [ 7 ] . For agents, higher reasoning effort gives equal or lower accuracy in 21 of 36 model–agent–benchmark combinations [ 29 ] , and neither sequential nor parallel scaling helps general agents much [ 31 ] . A concurrent report covers mathematics, science questions, and planning across nine models [ 3 ] . None of these studies combines mathematics, programming, and agent tasks with charged selection calls and a comparison against a stronger model, which is the combination SELF-POT provides. Cost-aware evaluation. Holistic evaluation suites report efficiency in runtime and hardware units [ 33 ] , agent evaluations argue for and adopt joint reporting of dollar cost and accuracy [ 30 , 29 ] , and cost-of-pass measures the expected dollar cost of one correct answer [ 19 ] . Test-time scaling studies mostly count FLOPs [ 47 , 53 ] , yet the unit of cost matters: inference demand changes the compute-optimal model size [ 44 ] , memory-access cost removes much of the apparent advantage of small models under best-of- N N sampling and long reasoning [ 43 ] , and models often reason far longer than a problem requires [ 9 , 24 ] . Cascades and routers instead choose a model for each query [ 8 , 55 , 23 , 1 , 16 , 41 , 15 ] , sometimes together with the number of samples [ 17 ] , and adaptive stopping rules reduce the samples a single model needs [ 2 , 32 , 14 ] . These approaches compare models at their native settings or assume that sampling a cheaper model is the more economical path, an assumption that SELF-POT tests directly. 6 Conclusion We introduced SELF-POT , a benchmark and evaluation framework that measures how additional inference becomes task success, and at what cost, across 350 sealed tasks in mathematics, programming, and agentic environments. A recurring lesson is that the most informative distinction lies between producing a correct candidate and successfully submitting it. On fixed programming pools, public-example selection raises correct submissions from 376 to 453, and output-preserving fallback alone recovers 61, so selection and failure handling can reverse an observed TTS loss. In mathematics, judging with fallback adds four correct submissions over cheaper voting, and discounted vote@3 adds a deployment trade-off, while Flash Direct retains the coding frontier. For agents, interfaces require validation before their outcomes can be attributed to planning. Together, these measurements connect candidate coverage, executable selection rules, and cost to the practical question of inference allocation: whether the next unit of budget is better spent on another candidate, a more reliable selection mechanism, or a different base model. Appendix B Test set construction Tasks were admitted by a model-independent eligibility check, drawn by stratum with a fixed seed, and sealed before any test-time call. Eligibility. Where an executable reference is distributed, eligibility requires that it succeeds and a blank or no-op submission fails under the pinned runtime. AppWorld uses the separate contract below because its test references are unavailable. For code, an official editorial program must pass every hidden test in our container; duplicate references are removed by code hash. AppWorld’s test split ships no reference solutions, so eligibility there requires the official development examples to pass, the native evaluator chain to be fixed, and a blank state to fail; all 585 test tasks met this contract. For Terminal-Bench, the Harbor oracle agent must obtain reward 1 and the nop agent reward 0; 62 of 66 tasks qualified, three were excluded for requiring GPUs, and one because its reference could not run in the shipped image. Sampling and exclusions. Within each source, tasks were stratified by published difficulty and sampled without replacement using seed 20260917, taking at most one task per scenario cluster or leakage group. Every task seen by any model during development (math 52, code 25, workflow 15, terminal 1) was excluded, together with three AtCoder contests held out as a whole (abc391, abc398, arc191). The set was sealed on 2026-09-21; the seal records hashes of the specification and of the public and private task files, and the tasks did not change afterwards.
